material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Solvent S and extractant X are independent benchmark labels, not real substance identities. Equal indices across the two fields imply no shared identity or property. The catalog provides no material-property estimates.

dossier.identity_policy: Solvent and extractant IDs are independent benchmark-only labels and do not identify real materials. Equal codes across the two fields have no meaning.
dossier.interpretation_policy: Treat the marginal profiles as incomplete prior evidence. They cannot identify the best pair without controlled pairwise experiments and do not reveal the objective score or optimal process settings.

property_scope.extractant: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous solvent reference panel.
property_scope.solvent: Marginal nominal distribution and selectivity tendencies aggregated across an anonymous extractant reference panel.

dossier.residual_policy: The solvent-extractant interaction table, world-level coefficient transform, phase-volume response, and mixing response are not disclosed. The hidden law is fixed for the entire campaign.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

# Partition campaign hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At a fixed phase-volume ratio and adequate mixing/settling, target fractions should follow a finite distribution-ratio relationship: organic fraction rises with organic phase share, with solvent–extractant pairing changing the effective distribution ratio. Marginal dossier values suggest S2 and X1–X3 may often favor target transfer, but pair interactions are unresolved.

## H2 [tentative]
Mixing may be kinetic: short/slow mixing could give incomplete equilibration, while sufficiently vigorous/long mixing should approach a plateau. A matched-condition comparison will test this; any effect smaller than the declared assay/HPLC noise remains unresolved.

## H3 [tentative]
Pre-separation HPLC should approximately close target inventory (organic + aqueous fractions), subject to sampling/noise. After retaining one phase, final assay should primarily report inventory in that retained phase rather than both phases.

## Planned discrimination
Use 12 independent batches from the same reagent charge: broad material-pair screening, controlled phase-amount contrasts, and matched mixing contrasts. Purchase one pre-separation HPLC per batch, then separate a declared phase, terminate, and final-assay it. Predictions are directional, not numerical, because the interaction, volume, and mixing laws are undisclosed.

# Partition campaign hypotheses

## H1 [supported within screened conditions; pairing interaction unresolved]
At nominally identical volumes (0.04 L solvent, 0.04 L aqueous addition, 0.02 L extractant) and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, pre-separation HPLC organic target fractions varied materially across pairings: about 0.123–0.314 (events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067, -0077). Differences well above the stated 0.015 channel noise indicate a material-pair effect, although the eight-point incomplete pairing screen cannot decompose solvent, extractant, and interaction effects. S0/X3 was highest among these observed combinations, but this is evidence about the screened set, not a general optimum.

The corresponding phase ratios clustered near 0.18–0.22, so phase-volume noise/variation is too small to explain the full organic-fraction spread. Target closure (organic + aqueous) is roughly near unity but varies with measurement noise/process proxy and must not be forced to exactly one.

## H2 [unresolved; prospective tests declared]
Using S0/X3 as a sensitive reference, increasing extractant volume at fixed total added liquid should increase phase ratio and organic target inventory. Planned contrasts: 0.01/0.05, 0.02/0.04, and 0.04/0.02 L extractant/aqueous addition, with solvent held at 0.04 L. A failure of organic fraction to rise beyond stated uncertainty would reject the simple finite-distribution picture in this scope.

At standard volumes, 1 s/100 rpm mixing is predicted to give less organic transfer than 300 s/600 rpm; 1200 s/1200 rpm is predicted to be near or above the standard response. If short and long conditions agree within uncertainty, mixing kinetics will remain unresolved or appear faster than the tested window.

## H3 [supported qualitatively]
Separation retains the requested phase rather than changing a sampling label. Organic-retained final assays largely preserve pre-separation organic target estimates (events -0010 through -0070). The aqueous-retained assay in batch 8 reports phase ratio 0 and high aqueous target inventory (runner-operation-0080), consistent with removal of the organic phase. Residual opposite-phase assay signals are treated as noise/sampling, not literal retained volume.

notes.text:
# Partition campaign hypotheses — final source-stage record

## H1 [supported in tested scope]
Target partition depends strongly on the anonymous solvent–extractant pairing. Under common phase additions and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, the eight screened pairs gave pre-separation HPLC organic inventories from 0.123 to 0.314 of initial target (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067, -0077; channel std 0.015). Phase ratios were only about 0.18–0.22, so their variation cannot plausibly account for the full pairing spread. Because the screen is incomplete and mostly changes solvent and extractant together, main effects versus interactions remain unresolved; anonymous IDs are categorical only.

## H2 [supported directionally; simple equilibrium constant is approximate]
For S0/X3 at 300 s/600 rpm, increasing extractant/aqueous addition from 0.01/0.05 to 0.02/0.04 to 0.04/0.02 L increased measured phase ratio from 0.094 to 0.218 to 0.409 and pre-separation organic target inventory from 0.183 to 0.314 to 0.560 (runner-operation-0087, -0047, -0097). This monotone change greatly exceeds channel noise and supports phase amount as a predictive driver.

A finite-distribution form is useful: normalized organic share is approximately (K r/[1-r+Kr]), where (r) is organic/total phase volume. Back-calculated apparent K values for the three phase-amount points are about 2.22, 1.64, and 1.80. Their scatter means one constant is only an approximate local summary, not an established law. Possible causes include process/sampling noise, concentration dependence, and incomplete equilibration.

## H3 [supported in tested mixing range]
At standard S0/X3 volumes, short/slow 1 s/100 rpm mixing gave organic target 0.263 (runner-operation-0107), intermediate 300 s/600 rpm gave 0.314 (runner-operation-0047), and long/vigorous 1200 s/1200 rpm gave 0.399 (runner-operation-0117). The short-to-long difference (0.136) exceeds the individual 0.015 channel noise; small phase-ratio differences do not explain it. Apparent K rose from about 1.33 to 2.63. Duration and speed were changed jointly, so their separate contributions and the equilibrium plateau are unresolved. Prediction within this tested family: more mixing energy/time tends to increase transfer, but extrapolation beyond 1200 s/1200 rpm is unsupported.

## H4 [supported qualitatively]
Phase retention behaves physically. Organic-retained final assays largely preserve the pre-separation organic inventory, while opposite-phase values are near the assay noise floor (for example runner-operation-0097 to -0100). Aqueous retention in batch 8 produced phase ratio 0, aqueous target 0.745, and organic target 0 (runner-operation-0080), consistent with removal of the organic layer. Hence phase-retention decisions should be based on which phase contains the desired inventory; pre-separation HPLC is the relevant two-phase reading.

## Evidence limits
All values are synthetic benchmark observations. HPLC and final assay consumed samples and have declared noise; observed closure need not equal one. Final assay occurs only after separation and termination and therefore must not be interpreted as a two-phase measurement. Only one aqueous-retention batch was run, most conditions lack replication, pairing coverage is incomplete, and no independent duration-versus-speed factorial was performed. These gaps limit causal separation and numerical precision.
notes.message: Final source-stage interpretation after all 12 batches

payload.report:
Observations: Twelve batches used the same 0.020 mol reagent charge. Each received a pre-separation HPLC measurement, a declared phase-retention step, termination, and a final assay. In the eight-pair screen, all at 0.040 L solvent, 0.040 L aqueous phase, 0.020 L extractant, 300 s/600 rpm mixing, and 300 s settling, the HPLC organic-target signal ranged from 0.123 to 0.314 while measured phase ratios remained in the much narrower 0.178–0.220 range. Specifically, batches 1–8 gave organic-target values of 0.123 (S0/X0), 0.244 (S1/X1), 0.180 (S2/X2), 0.259 (S3/X3), 0.314 (S0/X3), 0.230 (S1/X2), 0.239 (S2/X1), and 0.285 (S3/X0). These differences are large relative to the declared HPLC product-channel standard uncertainty of 0.015.

The controlled S0/X3 phase-amount series was monotonic. With extractant/aqueous additions of 0.010/0.050 L (batch 9), 0.020/0.040 L (batch 5), and 0.040/0.020 L (batch 10), HPLC phase ratio rose from 0.094 to 0.218 to 0.409, and organic-target signal rose from 0.183 to 0.314 to 0.560. A simple local distribution-ratio calculation gives apparent values of roughly 2.22, 1.64, and 1.80: similar enough to make a finite-partition model useful, but not constant enough to establish it as an exact law.

Mixing also mattered for S0/X3 at standard volumes. Batch 11, mixed for 1 s at 100 rpm, produced an HPLC organic-target signal of 0.263; batch 5 at 300 s/600 rpm produced 0.314; and batch 12 at 1200 s/1200 rpm produced 0.399. The short-to-long difference of 0.136 substantially exceeds measurement noise. Their phase ratios were only 0.213, 0.218, and 0.195, respectively, so phase-ratio variation does not explain the ordering.

Phase-retention measurements behaved consistently with physical removal of one layer. Organic-retained final assays generally reproduced the preceding organic inventory within process and measurement variation—for example, batch 10 changed from 0.560 by HPLC to 0.542 by final assay, with essentially no aqueous target remaining. Batch 8 deliberately retained the aqueous phase: its final assay reported phase ratio 0, aqueous target 0.745, organic target 0, impurity signal 0.476, and purity 0.587. In contrast, organic-retained batches generally had much lower impurity signals and approximately 0.88–0.93 purity. This indicates that, in the tested systems, the organic layer was usually the more target-selective layer, while much of the impurity burden remained aqueous. The high-extractant batch also showed a tradeoff: batch 10 achieved the largest organic target inventory, but its pre-separation impurity signal rose to 0.054 and purity fell to 0.869.

Inference: Partition is governed jointly by categorical solvent–extractant pairing, organic phase amount, and mass-transfer history. A useful qualitative representation is that every pair has an effective affinity for the organic phase; increasing the organic-phase share increases the target captured there, and stronger/longer mixing moves the system further toward its attainable partition state. S0/X3 had the largest organic-target signal among the eight screened standard-volume pairs, but that is an observed winner only within this incomplete screen, not evidence of a universal optimum. The sizable differences among pairs at nearly equal phase ratios demonstrate a material effect, while the S0/X3 volume series supports a finite-capacity partition response rather than a phase-ratio-only rule.

Contribution of supplied information: The nominal dossier was useful as a prior. It indicated that target distribution and selectivity varied across both solvent and extractant panels, suggested S2 and X1–X3 as generally promising marginal choices, and warned that the undisclosed interaction table and process responses could not be inferred from those marginals. The experiments supplied the missing pair-specific evidence. In particular, S0/X3 outperforming the tested S2 combinations shows why marginal rankings alone were insufficient and is consistent with a solvent–extractant interaction or context-dependent marginal behavior. The dossier’s high nominal target-to-impurity selectivities were qualitatively consistent with the organic-versus-aqueous retention results, but they did not determine the observed numerical partition.

Conjecture: The mixing series suggests approach toward equilibrium, with 1 s/100 rpm under-contacted and 1200 s/1200 rpm closer to equilibrium. However, no plateau was demonstrated. The scatter in apparent distribution ratios could arise from incomplete equilibration, concentration-dependent affinity, sampling/process variation, or a law more complex than a single constant. Increased extractant volume may also improve transfer through more than phase ratio alone, because it simultaneously changes extractant quantity and aqueous dilution.

Remaining uncertainty and scope: Solvent and extractant identities are anonymous benchmark categories, so no molecular mechanism is claimed. Only eight of sixteen pairings were examined, mostly without replication, preventing clean separation of solvent main effects, extractant main effects, and pair interactions. Mixing duration and speed were changed together, so their individual contributions are unidentified. The volume series changed extractant amount, aqueous amount, and phase ratio simultaneously. Settling time, solvent amount, reagent charge, and temperature range were not varied. Final assays were performed after separation and therefore validate retained-phase inventory rather than independently remeasure the original two-phase partition. Measurement noise, occasional imperfect mass closure, and process variability limit numerical precision. Accordingly, the conclusions are strongest for the tested volume and mixing ranges and should not be extrapolated to untested pairs or extreme conditions without further measurements.

payload.rationale: Predictions use the observed finite-partition response to extractant phase share, pair-specific behavior, and the measured increase in organic transfer with stronger or longer mixing. S0/X0 was weak in the direct screen, whereas S0/X3 was much stronger, so Q01 remains aqueous-dominant and Q06 exceeds Q05 organically. Intervals exclude random HPLC noise but include uncertainty from volume and mixing interpolation; they are wider for the untested S2/X0 and S2/X3 pairs and for speed-versus-duration extrapolation.

payload.report:
1. No batch-specific instance prior and no ground truth were supplied; the only prior was the marginal nominal material dossier. The least-established self-developed law is the approximate single distribution-ratio representation, especially its assumed transferability across mixing conditions and material pairs. Batches 5, 9, and 10 supported a monotonic phase-amount response for S0/X3, but their apparent ratios were not constant. Likewise, batches 5, 11, and 12 suggested a mixing effect, yet duration and speed changed together. Thus “approach to equilibrium with increased mixing” remains plausible rather than demonstrated, and the marginal dossier cannot validate untested individual pairs.

2. I would run S0/X3 at the batch-5 standard amounts, settle for 300 s, but mix for 1200 s at 600 rpm. I would measure pre-removal organic and aqueous target fractions and phase ratio by HPLC. Compared with batch 5, a clearly higher organic fraction would support a duration-dependent approach toward equilibrium; comparison with batch 12 would then help bound the additional contribution of speed. Agreement with batch 5 would make duration unimportant over 300–1200 s and shift the explanation toward stirring speed or between-batch variability. Agreement with batch 12 would imply duration dominated. A lower organic fraction would undermine the simple monotonic kinetic account and raise alternatives such as non-monotonic mixing, emulsion/settling effects, or uncontrolled process variability.

3. The nominal marginal distributions were underused quantitatively: they informed qualitative expectations but were not integrated into a calibrated interaction model. Impurity and purity observations—especially the impurity-rich retained aqueous phase in batch 8 and the purity tradeoff in high-extractant batch 10—were also secondary to the target-partition model. Final assays were used mainly to validate phase retention, not to estimate systematic HPLC-to-assay bias.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q07, Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2/X0 and S2/X3 were never directly tested; Q11–Q12 additionally require separating stirring-speed effects from duration. Q09–Q10 are also weak because the only S0/X0 observation was at one mixing condition. The report and predictions are directionally consistent, including the Q01 aqueous-retention decision and Q06-over-Q05 comparison. The main tension is that the report emphasized incomplete pair coverage, nonconstant apparent ratios, and confounded mixing variables, whereas the predictions necessarily assigned numerical values to untested S2 pairs and transferred a mixing response between pairs. Their wider intervals acknowledged but did not eliminate that extrapolation. The predictions also imposed complementary aqueous and organic point fractions, an additional conservation assumption not established as an exact empirical law by the noisy HPLC closures. This is a retrospective audit of the sealed outputs, not a modification of them.
